104.t: Friendship with Oscar Peterson, and Ed Thigpen's nervous start
104.s: She and Oscar stayed friendly, talking at the Hickory House about teaching kids; she recalls dinners in Vienna and Ed Thigpen's anxious early days in the trio.
104.q: But we were talking about Oscar. Since that time we’ve been as friendly as anybody can be with being on the road and only meeting here and there. I would go see him in clubs, and I remember he came to the Hickory House. As I say, he sat in, and we had a long conversation about music and different…

104.t: Choosing a dream band: trumpet, saxophones and bass
104.s: For her dream quintet she picks Roy Hargrove, Sonny Rollins, Phil Woods or Jerry Dodgion, and bassists George Mraz or Christian McBride.
104.ch: Dream band, reading and closing thoughts
104.q: Those that are still around, because of course I’m always thinking of a Sonny Stitt lookalike or Dexter Gordon lookalike.

104.t: Roy Haynes on drums and recapping the dream band
104.s: Roy Haynes is her only drummer choice; Williams recaps the band of Haynes, Mraz, Hargrove, Rollins and Woods with her on piano.
104.ch: Dream band, reading and closing thoughts
104.q: Roy Haynes. Roy Haynes. Roy Haynes. Roy Haynes. No doubt about it.

529.t: Rehearsing in Canada and learning Peterson's difficult trio parts
529.s: Sam flies to Canada to rehearse, tours small colleges, and struggles with the written unison parts but takes it as a challenge.
529.q: tour, you know, start playing some little towns, little schools, colleges and stuff all out west, and stuff, starting getting, started getting because this is quite an experience for me. I never played parts, these kind of parts before, playing things in unison and stuff.

529.t: Five and a half years with Peterson and playing 3/4 loose
529.s: The trio with Sam and Louis Hayes won attention, and their loose way of playing 3/4 time amazed Peterson and freed him.
529.q: ...and I wind up staying there 5½ years, you know, and the man never, did never win a poll as a group in his whole career, trio, and we hit the scene, you know, London House, and we started hitting all the places where the group performed,man, and everybody said man, that's the greatest trio, never…

741.t: Players he'd still like to play with
741.s: He wants to play with Jim Hall, Sonny Rollins and Elvin Jones.
741.q: Well I’ve always said I mean it’s probably because of my connection to Jim Hall and what he did with Sonny Rollins, I’ve gotten a chance to play with Jim, although I’d like to play with him a little more I mean maybe just one on one, that would be great. We’ve done some on concerts but it’s never…

536.t: The Oscar Peterson Trio and arranged music
536.s: Brown describes the trio as a peak in which his JATP experience came out, and why the group was so arranged after years of jamming.
536.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and the Oscar Peterson Trio
536.q: Yeah. It was a good era for all of us because this, after all of us being with Jazz at the Philharmonic and now we wind up with that group, there’s a lot of stuff that you have accrued over those years of playing with all those giants. And now all of this stuff can come out, and it comes out in…

742.t: His trio with Kenny Washington and Peter Washington
742.s: He has played two and a half years with the two Washingtons, whose natural connection needs little discussion.
742.q: Well my trio is Kenny Washington and Peter Washington. And we’ve been playing together for the last two and a half years or so. And there’s a very natural connection between us, a very natural feeling about what we care about, what are the central forces that we — just a sort of center current to…

606.t: The challenge of Oscar Peterson's trio arrangements
606.s: Six almost seven years with Peterson; complicated memorized arrangements pushed Ellis and Ray Brown to the limit.
606.q: Oh my gosh it’s hard to describe. We had a lot of arrangements and they weren’t just charts that you’ve got a head, they were really complicated. And you had to remember them all, because we didn’t write it down. And Oscar made, he didn’t purposely make it — but he used to know about how much Ray…

497.t: Best musical situations: McCoy Tyner quartet, his father and Roots
497.s: He calls the McCoy Tyner quartet his current favorite and describes his saxophone-quartet band Roots with Benny Golson and others.
497.q: One of the best? Oh there are a few. Well the one with McCoy is great. For me it’s great. I’m in a quartet situation so there’s a lot of freedom and it’s, again, playing with McCoy.

743.s: Gordon's dream band would include Hackett, Teagarden, Condon, Stacy, Wettling and Walter Page, with Russell and Marsala as clarinet subs.
743.q: Well I’d probably have Bobby Hackett or Jack Teagarden and Eddie Condon and Jess Stacy, George Wettling, Walter Page on bass maybe, and I’d have Pee Wee Russell and Joe Marsala as my alternate clarinet players whenever I couldn’t make it.

329.t: Benny Goodman trios and playing without a bass
329.s: Hanna admires Goodman's trio recordings and describes playing piano-drums trios with Peplowski, Varro, Sutton, Bunch and McKenna.
329.q: B.G., yeah. Yeah, he was great, great. He never cared for me, but gez, I heard some fantastic things he’s done. Still, even now, you’ll bring back some old things he did. My wife and I were listening to him on a tape, 1935, 1938 with Gene and Teddy. They had to divide it up and it was much better…

520.t: Oscar Peterson trio versus horn bands
520.s: Hayes found Peterson great but felt restricted in a star and co-star trio compared with Silver and Cannonball.

548.t: Musicians he would like to play with regularly
548.s: He would love sustained work with Smitty Smith, Corea, Hancock or Elvin Jones to grow as a player.

362.s: Mance wants players interacting rather than taking turns; the trio developed duo-style intimacy and sometimes adds a violinist.
362.q: Actually this trio is kind of different. And Junior really wanted to play talking together sometimes. Not this is a piano solo. Not this is a bass solo. But he wanted to play sometimes all together. Sometimes speak all together. You know he plays something, even if this is his solo, but I play…

515.t: The Bill Evans homage with Eddie Gomez and Paul Motian
515.s: Corea describes the open trio at the Blue Note, with Gomez and Motian as Evans alumni.
515.q: kind of hovering over the whole thing, because of the fact that every time I’ve ever worked with Eddie Gomez, it’s not possible to work with Eddie without being aware of his 11 years with Bill Evans—of course. And then Paul, my God, he made those seminal recordings that will be remembered forever…

370.t: Paul Motian's role at the Vanguard
370.s: Gordon remembers Paul Motian's death and the carte blanche booking and continuity he gave the club.

506.t: The Stryker trio with Russell Malone and Mulgrew Miller
506.s: Carter explains the drumless trio, its transparency and fragility.

376.s: He recalls playing Blue in Green with his quartet.
376.q: And Marc Johnson. And I asked him in the middle of a set, “Joey, [want to?] play on the solo?” He said, “Blue and green.” [laughs] The slow number.

233.t: The Montgomery brothers never really a trio
233.s: Their playing was always with drums or a horn because Wes and Buddy had too strong a pulse for light trio work.
233.ch: Mingus and the call from Hampton

There were a lot of times you might be working with three, four, five, whatever amount of pieces. We weren't just into it as a trio, really into it as a trio. As a…
